title: The Robot Gardener
summary: A community garden gets an experimental robot that at first cannot tell weeds from vegetables, until the kids who tend the garden teach it to see the difference.
poll: A machine that makes mistakes at first should be given a second chance to learn.

versions.title: The Robot Gardener
versions.text:
Lina and Yousef help in a garden. Rows of carrots and tomatoes grow there. We call them vegetables.

One day, a man comes to help. His name is Mr. Faisal. He brings a new robot. Its name is Sprout. Sprout can give the plants water. It can pull up weeds too.

But Sprout makes a mistake. It can not tell a weed from a plant. It pulls up a carrot. Then it pulls up a tomato too!

The kids feel sad. They go tell the man. He wants to help right away. They want to teach Sprout.

They show Sprout some cards. One card has a weed. One card has a carrot plant. The man helps Sprout learn from them. Soon Sprout can look at a leaf and know what it is.

Sprout stops pulling up the wrong plants. It only pulls real weeds now. The garden looks neat again. Lina, Yousef, and Sprout are now a team.

Lina and Yousef spend many days helping in a garden near their homes. Many people grow vegetables there. Long rows of carrots and tomatoes fill the garden. These vegetables need lots of water and weeding.

One day, a man named Mr. Faisal visits the garden. He carries something new with him. It is a small robot called Sprout. Sprout can water the plants by itself. It moves slowly along the rows. It can also pull up weeds without being told.

At first, though, Sprout makes a big mistake. It cannot yet tell a weed from a young vegetable plant. One morning, it pulls up a healthy carrot plant! A short while later, it pulls up a tomato plant too, and thinks the leaves are a weed.

Lina and Yousef feel upset when they find the pulled-up plants in the dirt. They hurry to tell Mr. Faisal what happened. He wants to fix the problem soon. The kids offer to help teach Sprout how to tell the plants apart.

Together, they show Sprout many cards. Some cards show common weeds. Other cards show young carrot and tomato plants. Mr. Faisal works with Sprout so it can learn something new each time. Little by little, Sprout learns to look at a leaf's shape before it acts.

After many weeks of practice, Sprout stops pulling up the wrong plants. It now pulls up only real weeds. Every vegetable plant stays untouched. The garden looks neat and full of life again, and Lina, Yousef, and Sprout have truly become a team.

versions.title: The Robot Gardener
versions.text:
Lina and Yousef spend many afternoons helping in a garden near their homes. Several families grow vegetables there side by side. Long, careful rows of carrots and tomatoes fill the garden. These vegetables need steady watering and regular weeding.

One afternoon, an engineer named Mr. Faisal arrives at the garden. He brings a small robot called Sprout. He built it to help with the garden's chores. Sprout can water the plants on its own. It rolls slowly along each row. It can also pull up weeds without being asked.

At first, however, Sprout makes a serious mistake. Its camera cannot yet recognize the difference between a stubborn weed and a young vegetable plant. One morning, it pulls up a healthy carrot plant, roots and all! A short while later, it pulls up a tomato seedling too, and thinks the leaves are a weed.

Lina and Yousef feel upset when they find the pulled-up plants lying in the dirt. They hurry to tell Mr. Faisal what has happened. He wants to fix the problem quickly. The two children offer to become his partners in teaching Sprout how to tell the plants apart.

Then, they show Sprout dozens of careful pictures. Some pictures show common weeds. Other pictures show young carrot and tomato plants at every stage of growth. Mr. Faisal adjusts Sprout's program so the robot can learn something useful from each picture. Little by little, Sprout learns to look at the shape and color of a leaf before it acts.

After many weeks of steady practice, Sprout stops pulling up the wrong plants. It now pulls up only real weeds, leaving every vegetable plant untouched. The garden looks neat and full of life once again, and Lina, Yousef, and Sprout have truly become a trusted garden team.

versions.title: The Robot Gardener
versions.text:
Lina and Yousef spend many afternoons volunteering in a busy community garden near their homes, where several neighborhood families cultivate vegetables side by side. Long, carefully tended rows of carrots and tomatoes fill the garden, and these vegetables require steady watering and regular weeding to thrive.

One afternoon, an engineer named Mr. Faisal arrives at the garden carrying an experimental machine he is eager to demonstrate. He introduces a small robot called Sprout, designed specifically to assist with the garden's many repetitive chores. Sprout can water the plants entirely on its own, rolling slowly along each row while its built-in sensors check the moisture in the soil. It can also pull up weeds without anyone needing to ask it twice.

At first, however, Sprout makes a significant mistake, because its onboard camera cannot yet distinguish between a stubborn weed and a young, delicate vegetable plant. One morning, it reaches down and pulls up a perfectly healthy carrot plant, roots and all, simply because the leaves resemble a common weed. A short while later, it pulls up a tender tomato seedling as well, mistaking its soft leaves for an ordinary weed.

Lina and Yousef feel genuinely upset when they discover the pulled-up plants scattered across the dirt path. They hurry to tell Mr. Faisal exactly what has happened to their vegetables. He wants to resolve the problem as quickly as possible. The two children offer to collaborate with him, teaching Sprout how to tell the different plants apart.

Working together as a small team, they show Sprout dozens of carefully chosen photographs: images of common weeds, and images of young carrot and tomato plants at every stage of growth. Mr. Faisal patiently calibrates Sprout's sensors and adjusts its program so the robot can learn something useful from each new photograph. Little by little, Sprout learns to examine the exact shape, size, and color of a leaf before deciding whether or not to pull it.

After several weeks of steady, patient practice, Sprout adapts completely and stops pulling up the wrong plants altogether. It now pulls up only genuine weeds, leaving every vegetable plant untouched and healthy. The garden looks neat and full of life once again, and Lina, Yousef, and Sprout have truly become a reliable, trusted gardening team that the whole neighborhood now depends on.

versions.title: The Robot Gardener
versions.text:
Lina and Yousef spend countless afternoons volunteering in a busy community garden near their homes, where several neighborhood families cultivate vegetables side by side in neat, shared plots that the entire community helps to maintain. Long, carefully tended rows of carrots and tomatoes fill the garden, and these vegetables require steady watering and regular weeding to thrive throughout the entire growing season.

One afternoon, an engineer named Mr. Faisal arrives at the garden carrying an experimental machine that he is eager to demonstrate to the children who faithfully tend the plots. He introduces a small robot called Sprout, designed specifically to assist with the garden's many repetitive chores, from watering each row methodically to weeding between the plants. Sprout can water the plants entirely on its own, rolling slowly along each row while its built-in sensors measure the moisture level in the soil. It can also pull up weeds without anyone needing to ask it twice.

At first, however, Sprout makes a significant and rather embarrassing mistake, because its onboard camera cannot yet reliably distinguish between a stubborn weed and a young, delicate vegetable plant growing nearby. One morning, it reaches down and pulls up a perfectly healthy carrot plant, roots and all, simply because the leaves happen to resemble the general shape of a common weed. A short while later, it pulls up a tender tomato seedling as well, mistaking its soft leaves for an ordinary garden weed rather than a valuable crop.

Lina and Yousef feel genuinely upset when they discover the pulled-up plants scattered across the dirt path between the rows of vegetables, worried that more damage might follow. They hurry to tell Mr. Faisal exactly what has happened to their carefully grown plants. He wants to resolve the problem as quickly as possible, so the two children offer to collaborate with him directly, helping to teach Sprout methodically how to tell the different kinds of plants apart.

Working together as a small, dedicated team, they show Sprout dozens of carefully chosen photographs: images of common weeds found around the garden, and images of young carrot and tomato plants at every stage of their growth, from tiny seedlings to fuller, more mature plants. Mr. Faisal patiently calibrates Sprout's sensors and adjusts its program line by line so the robot can learn something useful from each new photograph it studies, gradually building a clearer internal picture of what each type of plant actually looks like. Little by little, Sprout learns to examine the exact shape, size, and color of a leaf before deciding whether or not to pull it from the ground.

After several weeks of steady, patient practice, Sprout adapts completely and stops pulling up the wrong plants altogether, its mistakes growing fewer with each passing day until they disappear entirely. It now pulls up only genuine weeds, leaving every vegetable plant untouched and healthy as it continues to grow toward a successful harvest. The garden looks neat and full of life once again, and Lina, Yousef, and Sprout have truly become a reliable, trusted gardening team that the whole neighborhood now depends on every single season.

versions.title: The Robot Gardener
versions.text:
Lina and Yousef devote countless afternoons to volunteering in a bustling community garden near their homes, where several neighborhood families cultivate vegetables side by side in neat, shared plots that the entire community works together to maintain throughout the year. Long, meticulously tended rows of carrots and tomatoes fill the garden, and these vegetables require steady watering and regular weeding if they are to thrive throughout the entire growing season, from the earliest seedlings to the final, bountiful harvest.

One afternoon, an engineer named Mr. Faisal arrives at the garden carrying an experimental machine that he is eager to demonstrate to the children who faithfully tend the plots day after day. He introduces a small robot called Sprout, designed specifically to assist with the garden's many repetitive chores, watering each row methodically and weeding carefully between the plants without complaint. Sprout can water the plants entirely on its own, rolling slowly along each row while its built-in sensors measure the moisture level in the soil, and it can likewise pull up weeds without anyone needing to ask it twice.

At first, however, Sprout makes a significant and rather embarrassing mistake, since its rudimentary onboard camera cannot yet reliably distinguish between a stubborn weed and a young, delicate vegetable plant growing just beside it. One morning, it reaches down and pulls up a perfectly healthy carrot plant, roots and all, simply because the leaves happen to resemble the general shape of a common weed. A short while later, it pulls up a tender tomato seedling as well, mistaking its soft leaves for an ordinary garden weed rather than a valuable crop worth protecting carefully.

Lina and Yousef feel genuinely upset when they discover the pulled-up plants scattered across the dirt path between the rows of vegetables, their hard work seemingly undone in a single morning. They hurry to tell Mr. Faisal exactly what has happened to their carefully grown plants, worried that further damage might follow if nothing changes soon. He wants to resolve the problem as quickly as possible, so the two children offer to collaborate with him directly, helping to teach Sprout methodically how to distinguish the different kinds of plants from one another.

Working together as a small, dedicated team, they show Sprout dozens of carefully chosen photographs: images of common weeds found throughout the garden, and images of young carrot and tomato plants at every stage of their growth, from tiny seedlings to fuller, more mature plants ready for harvest. Mr. Faisal patiently calibrates Sprout's sensors and adjusts its program line by line so the robot can extract something useful from each new photograph it studies, gradually building a clearer internal picture of precisely what each type of plant actually looks like up close. Little by little, Sprout learns to examine the exact shape, size, and color of a leaf before ever deciding whether or not to pull it from the ground.

After several weeks of steady, patient practice, Sprout adapts completely and stops pulling up the wrong plants altogether, its mistakes growing fewer with each passing day until they disappear entirely from its daily routine. It now pulls up only genuine weeds, leaving every vegetable plant untouched and flourishing as it continues to grow toward a successful harvest. The garden looks neat and full of life once again, and Lina, Yousef, and Sprout have truly become a reliable, trusted gardening team that the whole neighborhood now depends on every single season.

The experience teaches Lina and Yousef a profound lesson about patience and collaboration: even a carefully engineered machine can make mistakes at first, but with consistent teaching and thoughtful adjustment, it can eventually become an invaluable partner rather than a persistent source of frustration, a lesson the two children carry with them well beyond the garden itself.

keyWords.definition: a machine that can do jobs by itself
keyWords.example: The robot in the factory moved boxes all day.

keyWords.definition: a piece of land where people grow plants
keyWords.example: My grandmother keeps roses in her garden.

keyWords.definition: a wild plant that grows where people do not want it
keyWords.example: Dad pulled a tall weed out of the flower bed.

keyWords.definition: a plant, or part of a plant, that people eat
keyWords.example: Onions and spinach are vegetables we eat at dinner.

keyWords.definition: to help someone or something learn
keyWords.example: My older sister likes to teach me new card games.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A trip the children take to a farm far away
A game two children play after school
A robot that learns to tell weeds from vegetables
How to build a robot from a kit
questions.why: The story follows Sprout the robot as it makes a mistake with the plants and then learns to tell weeds from vegetables.

wrong.A: The story happens in a community garden, not on a trip to a farm.
wrong.B: The story is not about a game the children play.
wrong.D: The story does not explain how to build a robot.

questions.stem: What is Sprout's job in the garden?
options: To plant new trees
To water plants and pull weeds
To paint the garden fence
To sell vegetables at a market
questions.why: The story says Sprout can water the plants and can also pull up weeds.

wrong.A: The story does not mention planting trees.
wrong.C: The story does not mention painting a fence.
wrong.D: The story does not say Sprout sells anything.

questions.stem: What mistake does Sprout make at first?
options: It pulls up good plants by mistake
It waters the garden much too often
It breaks part of the garden fence
It forgets to turn itself on some mornings
questions.why: The story says Sprout pulls up a carrot plant and a tomato plant, thinking they are weeds.

wrong.B: The story does not say Sprout waters too much.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a fence.
wrong.D: Sprout is working, not off, when it makes its mistake.

questions.stem: Why do Lina and Yousef feel sad when they find the pulled-up plants?
options: They do not like gardens at all, even in the spring
They wanted Sprout to water less on hot afternoons
They worked hard to grow those vegetables
They were hoping for rain all week for the new seeds
questions.why: Lina and Yousef help in the garden, so losing the carrot and tomato plants they cared for makes them upset.

wrong.A: They clearly like the garden, since they spend afternoons helping there.
wrong.B: The story is not about how much Sprout waters.
wrong.D: The story does not mention hoping for rain.

questions.stem: Why does Mr. Faisal want to fix Sprout's mistake quickly?
options: So he can sell Sprout to someone else
So the robot does not pull up more good plants
So the children will stop visiting the garden
So the robot can leave the garden forever
questions.why: Since Sprout already pulled up healthy plants by mistake, fixing the problem quickly keeps the rest of the garden safe.

wrong.A: The story does not mention selling Sprout.
wrong.C: The children want to stay and help, not leave.

LOW.modelAnswer: I think Lina and Yousef were right to help teach Sprout. At first, Sprout pulled up a carrot plant and a tomato plant by mistake, which was a problem. MID.modelAnswer: Lina, Yousef, and Mr. Faisal worked as a team to fix Sprout's mistake. First, the children noticed that Sprout had pulled up a carrot plant and a tomato plant, and they told Mr. Faisal right away. Then they all showed Sprout many photographs of weeds and young vegetable plants while Mr. Faisal adjusted its program. Because everyone worked together, Sprout learned to recognize plants correctly and became a trusted partner in the garden.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says a machine that makes mistakes at first should be given a second chance to learn. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Sprout's mistakes and how it improved.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that a machine making mistakes at first should get a second chance to learn. Sprout pulled up healthy carrot and tomato plants because its camera could not yet distinguish them from weeds, but that early failure did not mean it was useless. Once Mr. Faisal calibrated its sensors and the children collaborated by showing it photographs, Sprout adapted and became a dependable partner in the garden. Someone might argue that a machine causing damage should simply be removed, but Sprout's story shows that patient correction can turn an experimental failure into a valuable success.
